item.title: A thermal microwave bus for neutral atom quantum computing
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Bichromatic Raman gate mediating interaction via a 3D microwave cavity virtually populates Rydberg states and cancels dispersive shifts, reaching gate fidelity F=0.997.

Grade 0.490 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “neutral atom tweezer arrays and Rydberg blockade entangling gates” · Matthew J. H. Kendall, Christopher J. Watson, Michael Ben Shem, Jonathan D. Breeze

Figure

Error-correction round time plotted against code distance d for the toric code and gross code, comparing purely shuttling-based qubit movement with the hybrid cavity-bus scheme.

Asks

Can microwave cavity-mediated entangling gates overcome the shuttling-time bottleneck and thermal sensitivity in neutral-atom arrays at finite cryogenic temperatures?

Before

was 0.76 for optical cavity deterministic CZ gates (Steiner 2023)

But

Numerical open-system simulations of up to 4 atoms, analytical Magnus-expansion bounds, requires cryogenic temperatures (T≲1 K) and high-Q cavity (Q>109).

Tools

3D re-entrant microwave cavity · Open quantum system Lindblad simulations · Schrieffer-Wolff perturbation theory · Optical tweezer array

Abstract

High-fidelity two-qubit gates in neutral-atom arrays rely on the Rydberg blockade, which is intrinsically short ranged and requires long range connectivity to be achieved through atom shuttling. We propose a four level architecture, where the typical ground state qubit can be leveraged for its long lifetime and the Rydberg states couple to a microwave cavity, allowing for long range cavity mediated gates. We first find the thermal dependence of two established protocols, the dispersive iSWAP native to the Tavis-Cummings model and the Controlled phase gate generated from driving the cavity. We simulate them under the presence of Rydberg decay, thermal photons, finite cavity linewidth and find fidelities which accompany closed form bounds. We then introduce the bichromatic Raman gate, which only virtually populates the Rydberg states and cancels dispersive shifts to mitigate both atomic and cavity decay, achieving a fidelity of F = 0.997. Finally, we consider a full optical tweezer array in a microwave cavity, and show that using a cavity mediated gate to close the periodic boundaries of the toric code shortens an error correction round by a factor of 2.3 for realistic array sizes. This was then applied to the wider family of Bivariate bicycle codes, and we find that it shortens a round of the gross code by a factor of 4.8.

item.title: Deterministic synthesis and processing of frequency-bin qubits in a macroscopically coherent quantum memory
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Cavity-assisted quantum memory using pre-created long-lived macroscopic spin coherence synthesizes and stores arbitrary frequency-bin photonic qubits using only RF rotations via spectrally nonlocal impedance matching.

Grade 0.483 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling” · S. A. Moiseev

Figure

Panel (a) shows the 5-level rare-earth ion level scheme and the optical/RF pulse timing sequence. Panel (b) shows the crystal inside a dual-mode optical resonator controlled by an RF coil.

Asks

Can pre-created long-lived macroscopic spin coherence in a cavity-assisted quantum memory be used to deterministically synthesize, store, and process arbitrary frequency-bin photonic states without optical pulse shaping?

Before

Extends the single-spin-coherence PLMC protocol (Moiseev 2024), which required optical controls and stored only single-frequency photonic states.

But

Spectral width of input pulse must be much smaller than inhomogeneous absorption linewidth and cavity linewidth (δωs≪Δin,κ2,3); requires strongly correlated inhomogeneous optical broadening and negligible ground-state spin dephasing during the protocol.

Tools

Pre-created Long-lived Macroscopic (PLM) spin coherence · Dual-mode optical cavity · Rare-earth-ion-doped crystals · Spectrally nonlocal impedance matching · Heisenberg-Langevin input-output formalism

Abstract

Quantum information processing requires efficient storage and manipulation of photonic states.Here, we advance a cavity-assisted quantum memory protocol based on Pre-created Long-lived Macroscopic (PLM) coherence, thereby transforming quantum memory from a passive storage device into a platform for deterministic in-memory photonic processing. It is demonstrated that spin PLM coherence enables all-optical control of quantum memory using robust radio-frequency rotations alone. Here, the spin coherence serves as a distributed coherent quantum bus, which mediates the deterministic synthesis and storage of frequency-bin states through spectrally nonlocal impedance matching. We identify an inherent time-reversal symmetry in the underlying dynamical equations, ensuring unitary evolution of the quantum memory operations. The presented results demonstrate a unified platform for quantum storage and optical signal processing, enabling controlled manipulation of frequency-bin photonic qubits and paving the way for scalable multimode quantum networks based on spectral-encoding architectures.

item.title: Anomalously enhanced lifetimes of low angular momentum Rydberg states in singly charged alkaline-earth metal ions
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Lifetimes of low angular momentum Rydberg P states in singly charged alkaline-earth metal ions are enhanced by factors >8 relative to Hydrogenic scaling predictions, approaching neutral alkali-metal atom lifetimes. In 40Ca+, P-state lifetimes are up to ∼20 times higher than S states with the same principal quantum number.

Grade 0.440 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Simon Euchner, Weibin Li, Igor Lesanovsky

Figure

Computed Rydberg S and P state lifetimes of 85Rb and 88Sr+ alongside their ratio versus principal quantum number n at T=0K and T=300K, showing deviation of P states from the predicted Hydrogenic scaling ratio of 16.

Asks

Do Rydberg states in singly charged alkaline-earth metal ions strictly follow the Hydrogenic scaling law that predicts a 16-fold lifetime reduction compared to neutral alkali-metal atoms?

Before

Hydrogenic scaling τ(Zeff)∝Zeff−4 predicted ionic Rydberg state lifetimes are reduced by a factor of 16 relative to neutral atoms.

But

Calculations assume single active valence electron in parametric model potentials within the dipole approximation, tested for n=20 to 80 at T=0K and T=300K.

Tools

Parametric model potentials · AlkCalc single-electron Hamiltonian diagonalisation · Einstein-A radiative rate calculations · Black-body radiation transition model

Abstract

Trapped ions excited to high-lying electronic states, so-called Rydberg states, open new opportunities for quantum simulation and quantum computing. Generally, the fidelity of quantum coherent operations critically depends on the longevity of Rydberg states. However, scaling laws predict that the lifetimes of Rydberg states in singly charged alkaline-earth metal ions are 16 times shorter, compared to their neutral atom counterparts. Here, we show that this is not generally the case. We report an anomalous lifetime enhancement of certain low angular momentum ionic Rydberg series by factors larger than eight. The anomaly is present at both zero and finite temperature, although it is caused by different mechanisms. At zero temperature, the anomalously enhanced lifetimes are caused by accidental cancellations of the relevant dipole transition matrix elements, while at room temperature the anomaly originates from the enlarged energetic separation of ionic Rydberg levels with respect to neutral-atom levels.

item.title: Quantum Mpemba effect from Stark localization
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Combining Wannier-Stark localization with local dissipative hopping induces a quantum Mpemba effect where localized single-particle lifetimes scale super-exponentially as τj≈1γ[(j−2)!]2(Δ/J)2(j−2) for γ≪Δ.

Grade 0.440 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Nico Albert, Masudul Haque, Shovan Dutta

Figure

Energy versus time for states initialized at different lattice sites j, showing faster relaxation for higher-energy states near the dissipative site, alongside quantum jump trajectories and perturbation-theory timescale predictions.

Asks

How can an energy landscape with local dissipation be designed in a quantum system to produce an anomalous relaxation hierarchy analogous to the classical Mpemba effect?

But

Strong-localization regime J/Δ≲1, local Markovian jump dissipation restricted to an isolated boundary site.

Tools

Wannier-Stark localization · Lindblad master equation · Quantum trajectory unraveling · Padé interpolation perturbation theory

Abstract

In classical systems, rugged potential energy landscapes provide a transparent mechanism for the celebrated Mpemba effect, in which hotter initial states cool down faster. This picture generally does not survive in quantum systems. Here we show how to design a quantum energy landscape with local dissipation leading to an Mpemba effect with parametrically separated timescales. Our approach uses Stark localization to design an energy landscape and localized incoherent hopping as cooling mechanism. The hops are triggered by rare "detection" events whose rate grows with energy, allowing hotter states to cool faster and producing super-exponentially separated cooling rates for localized initial states. We further show that the effect is dramatically enhanced by collective hopping of bound pairs in the presence of attractive on-site interactions. These findings have clear experimental signatures accessible in present-day setups.

item.title: Collective cavity quantum electrodynamics in solid-state optical clocks
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Extracting clock error from collective nuclear coherence through resonator field enables clock cycle reset on fast decoherence timescale (1/γz) rather than long radiative lifetime (1/γ). Instability is minimized when collective cooperativity CN=1 in the low-saturation limit and CN,opt=1+4Ω2/(6γγ⟂) under saturation.

Grade 0.431 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons” · Karen Mamian, Georgy A. Kazakov, Thorsten Schumm, Charles Roques-Carmes

Figure

Fractional frequency instability σyτ as a function of pump power P1 and thorium density ρTh, showing the analytical optimal power curve (dashed green), optimal collective cooperativity (dashed orange), and the mean-field bistability boundary (red).

Asks

How can collective cavity quantum electrodynamics overcome the mismatch between short nuclear coherence time and long radiative lifetime in solid-state 229Th clocks?

Before

TU Wien nuclear clock absorption spectroscopy achieved σy(τ=1 s)=3×10−12 using N∼1016 nuclei; proposed cavity scheme matches instability with N∼1011 nuclei.

But

Mean-field theory in the bad-cavity regime (κ2≫4G2N/κ2). Assumes homogeneous coupling via phase matching and CaF2 host parameters with γ=1.59×10−3 s−1.

Tools

Born-Markov master equation · mean-field cumulant expansion · whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) cavity QED · two-photon optonuclear quadrupolar (ONQ) pumping

Abstract

Solid-state frequency standards are generally limited by strong decoherence, rendering conventional interrogation schemes inefficient. The ²²⁹Th nuclear clock provides a unique and timely platform for solid-state optical metrology and nuclear cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED), featuring a coherence time many orders of magnitude shorter than the radiative lifetime in current experiments. Here, we propose and analyze three cavity QED-enhanced clock interrogation schemes that turn this timescale mismatch into an advantage, leveraging collective coupling of thorium nuclei to nanophotonic modes to enable fast interrogation and detection despite the long population lifetime. We reveal the central role of collective cooperativity in determining the clock frequency instability, and derive the optimal conditions (power, working-point detuning, thorium density) for clock operation.

item.title: Nonequilibrium energy transport and fluctuations in two-photon-driven nonlinear quantum optical systems
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Two-photon driving strongly enhances the drive input energy current and signal-to-noise ratio via multiphoton resonances ωd(m)≃ω0+(2m−1)U, substantially modifying non-Gaussian higher-order current cumulants compared to single-photon driving.

Grade 0.431 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Y. T. Chen, Y. W. Lu, J. C. Lu, C. Wang

Figure

Drive input energy current log10⁡(JP), second-order fluctuations log10⁡(Jl(2)), and signal-to-noise ratio 𝒮l versus drive frequency ωd, showing enhancement when two-photon loss is added to single-photon dissipation.

Asks

How two-photon driving reorganizes nonlinear dressed-state transitions to control nonequilibrium average energy current and higher-order current fluctuations in open quantum optical systems.

But

Weak-driving regime, low-energy three-state approximation, Ohmic spectral density.

Tools

rotating-frame driven quantum master equation · full counting statistics · dressed-state eigenbasis expansion

Abstract

Understanding nonequilibrium transport and fluctuations driven by nonclassical light in nonlinear quantum optical systems is challenging. Here, we formulate a driven quantum master equation in the rotating frame combined with full counting statistics, retaining the drive-induced frequency shifts in the system-reservoir interactions and providing a unified description of drive-assisted incoherent transitions based on the rotated system dressed-basis. Applied to a Kerr resonator and a nonlinear Jaynes-Cummings model, the approach reveals pronounced multiphoton-resonant enhancement of the drive input energy current, with significant high peaks under two-photon driving compared to the single-photon case. The two-photon resonance relations are analytically obtained. Resonance structure in the nonlinear Jaynes-Cummings model nonlinearly relies on qubit-photon couplings, with additional dressed-state branches. A low-energy-state approximation attributes the resonant current enhancement to dressed-state hybridization and efficient activation of incoherent energy exchange processes. Beyond the average current, two-photon-driving induced energy exchange picture near resonance also substantially modifies the second-order current fluctuation and higher-order current cumulant, while increasing the time-normalized signal-to-noise ratio. Adding two-photon loss introduces extra incoherent photon-pair exchange pathways and further reshapes the current and its fluctuations. We hope these results may deepen interpretation of photon driving and quantum dissipation cooperatively governing nonequilibrium energy transport and fluctuations.

item.title: Gaussian quantum reservoir computing with a hybrid cavity magnomechanical system
item.description:
Worth a look new result — A 4-mode hybrid cavity magnomechanical system operated in the linearized Gaussian regime enables quantum reservoir computing and delayed signal reconstruction using quadrature fluctuation covariance features. For finite measurement budgets (Nm=1010 shots), intermediate encoding strength ϵΔ minimizes reconstruction error.

Grade 0.431 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling” · Hajar Assil, Khadija El Anouz, Abderrahim El Allati, Gian Luca Giorgi

Figure

Delayed signal reconstruction NMSE plotted against delay τ and encoding strength ϵΔ/2π across finite measurement counts Nm=104 to 1010 versus ideal limit Nm→∞, revealing a statistical trade-off minimum in reconstruction error.

Asks

Can a hybrid cavity magnomechanical platform act as a continuous-variable Gaussian quantum reservoir computer when driven through an auxiliary-cavity detuning port?

But

Linearized Gaussian regime at T=50 mK; offline state tomography without continuous-measurement back-action; numerical simulation.

Tools

quantum Langevin equations · covariance matrix feature extraction · ridge regression linear readout · Wishart finite-sampling statistics

Abstract

We propose a quantum reservoir computing framework based on a hybrid cavity magnomechanical system in the linearized Gaussian regime. The reservoir combines microwave-cavity, magnon, and mechanical degrees of freedom, and is extended by an auxiliary cavity acting as an input port, with time-dependent signals encoded in its detuning. The covariance matrix of the quadrature fluctuations provides the features for a trained linear readout. Using linear-memory, nonlinearmemory, and parity-check benchmarks, we find strong temporal memory together with more limited nonlinear processing, whose balance is controlled by the reservoir evolution time, and we show that intermode correlations substantially enhance the information accessible to the readout. The same architecture reconstructs a time-dependent signal encoded in the auxiliary-cavity detuning, with an accuracy governed by the interplay between the internal couplings and the encoding strength, and robust against Gaussian detuning noise. Accounting for finite measurement statistics reveals a trade-off between encoding strength and the precision of the covariance estimation, so that the optimal encoding depends on the available measurement budget. These results establish hybrid cavity magnomechanical systems as a promising platform for continuous-variable quantum reservoir computing with potential applications in signal probing.

item.title: A four-state quantum communication protocol with mesoscopic twin beams
item.description:
Worth a look incremental — Twin-beam communication alphabet extended from 2 to 4 states (2 bits per use) using superimposed thermal noise, with record-and-resend attacks detected at 90% probability for attacked fractions f≈0.10 to 0.40 across block sizes N=8×104 down to 5×103.

Grade 0.425 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks” · Stefano Carsi

Figure

Detection probability of record-and-resend attack versus attacked fraction f across block sizes N=5×103, 2×104, and 8×104, compared to a 5% false-alarm baseline.

Asks

Can a twin-beam quantum communication protocol be extended from binary to four-state encoding while retaining eavesdropping detection via the noise reduction factor?

Before

Binary hybrid encoding scheme by Razzoli et al. [4] delivering 1 bit per symbol using mean photon number with noise reduction factor R as a security witness.

But

Channel detection efficiency η=9.0±3%; state discrimination on R limited by calibration mismatch and test statistics fluctuations; communication evaluated on bootstrapped blocks from stored datasets rather than live independent transmissions.

Tools

mesoscopic twin-beam parametric down-conversion source · silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) · rotating ground-glass diffuser for thermal noise generation · single-arm Fano factor (⟨m⟩, F) threshold decoding and ML classifiers · noise reduction factor eavesdropping monitoring

Abstract

Twin-beam (TWB) states generated by parametric down-conversion exhibit strong photon-number correlations that can be exploited for quantum communication. In the mesoscopic regime, these correlations can be directly investigated using photon-number-resolving detectors, such as silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). Their nonclassical nature is quantified by the noise reduction factor (NRF), which provides a witness of quantum correlations and a means of monitoring channel security. In this work, a quantum communication protocol based on TWB states, originally proposed for binary encoding, is extended to a four-state scheme capable of transmitting two bits per use. Information is encoded by combining two mean photon-number values and two mode numbers of thermal noise superimposed on one arm of the twin beam, defining four distinguishable states in the (m,R) plane. While the mean detected photon number enables the retrieval of one bit, the NRF provides discrimination of the second bit and a security check against intercept-and-resend attacks, which introduce additional noise and degrade the quantum correlations. The protocol is investigated through two experimental measurement campaigns. First, the twin-beam source is characterized in terms of photon-number statistics, NRF, and detection efficiency to establish the operating conditions of the communication channel. Subsequently, the four-state protocol is implemented and evaluated through the analysis of state distributions and their 95% confidence regions, error probability as a function of sample size, and a comparative assessment of machine learning classifiers for state discrimination. Finally, the response of the NRF to an intercept-and-resend attack is investigated to assess the protocol's ability to detect eavesdropping.
